pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📐 **Strand 3 — Geometry And Measurement**
Shape, space, measurement, position and movement — the mathematics of the world around us.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B7.3.2)
- B7.3.2.1 — Demonstrate the ability to find the perimeter of plane shapes, including circles, using the concept of pi (π) to find the circumference of a circle. B7.3.2.2 — Derive the formula for determining the area of a triangle and use it to solve problems.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- find perimeters of shapes whose sides are given in two units
- name the parts of a circle and discover π from measurements
- use C = πd = 2πr to find the circumference of a circle
- draw rectangles and triangles of given dimensions and areas on a square grid
- derive and use the formula Area of triangle = [[1/2]] × base × height

pages.title: Perimeter with mixed units
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Calculate the perimeter of given shapes whose dimensions are in two units (cm and mm, m and cm, or km and m).
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.1.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Perimeter** — The **perimeter** of a shape is the total distance around its boundary. Before adding the lengths, change them all to the **same unit**.
| **Conversion** | **Facts** |
|---|---|
| Length | 10 mm = 1 cm; 100 cm = 1 m; 1,000 m = 1 km |
| Examples | 7 cm 5 mm = 7.5 cm = 75 mm; 1 m 75 cm = 1.75 m; 2 km 300 m = 2,300 m = 2.3 km |
## ✏️ Example 10.1
Find the perimeter of the triangular plot of land shown.
[[fig:m7-f50]]
Figure 10.1: A triangular plot of land
**Solution**
Convert to metres (the smaller unit): 2 km 300 m = 2,300 m; 1 km 850 m = 1,850 m; 950 m.
Perimeter = 2,300 + 1,850 + 950 = **5,100 m** (= 5.1 km)
## ✏️ Example 10.2
A rectangle measures 7 cm 5 mm by 4 cm 8 mm. Find its perimeter in centimetres.
**Solution**
Convert to decimals of the larger unit: 7 cm 5 mm = 7.5 cm; 4 cm 8 mm = 4.8 cm.
Perimeter = 2 × (7.5 + 4.8) = 2 × 12.3 = **24.6 cm**
## ✏️ Example 10.3
A classroom floor is 4 m 25 cm long and 3 m 75 cm wide. Find the length of skirting board needed to go round it (ignore the door).
**Solution**
4 m 25 cm = 4.25 m; 3 m 75 cm = 3.75 m.
Perimeter = 2 × (4.25 + 3.75) = 2 × 8 = **16 m**

pages.body:

lessons.title: The circle and π

pages.title: The circle and π
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Use the relationships between the diameter and the circumference to deduce the formula for finding the circumference of a circle and use it to solve problems.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.1.2
## Parts of a circle
[[fig:m7-f51|Figure 10.2: Parts of a circle]]
| **Part** | **Meaning** |
|---|---|
| Centre (O) | the fixed point in the middle |
| Radius (r) | a line from the centre to the circle |
| Diameter (d) | a chord through the centre; d = 2r |
| Circumference (C) | the distance round the circle (its perimeter) |
| Chord | a straight line joining two points on the circle |
| Arc | part of the circumference |
| Sector | the region between two radii and an arc |
| Segment | the region between a chord and an arc |
## Discovering π
> 🧪 **Activity 10.1 — Measuring circular objects**
1. Collect circular objects: tins, cups, bowls, a bicycle tyre, the base of a bucket.
2. Measure the **diameter** with a ruler (across the widest part, through the centre).
3. Measure the **circumference** by wrapping a string or tape measure round the object, then straightening the string against a ruler.
4. Record your results in a table and calculate C ÷ d for each object. What do you notice?
## ✏️ Example 10.4
Complete the table and comment on the results of C ÷ d.
| **Circle** | **Circumference (C) cm** | **Diameter (d) cm** | **C ÷ d** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tin A | 13 | 4 |  |
| Tin B | 38 | 12 |  |
**Solution**
Tin A: 13 ÷ 4 = **3.25**; Tin B: 38 ÷ 12 ≈ **3.17**.
For every circle, C ÷ d is a little more than 3. Careful measurement shows that the ratio is always the same number, called **π (pi)**:
π = [[C/d]] ≈ 3.141592… ≈ 3.142 ≈ [[22/7]]

pages.title: Example 10.5
pages.body:
> ✨ **Did you know?** π cannot be written exactly as a fraction or as a decimal that ends or repeats. Mathematicians in ancient Egypt, Babylon, Greece (Archimedes) and China all found approximations for π. Today computers have calculated π to trillions of decimal places! Research the history of π on the internet.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Circumference of a circle** — Since [[C/d]] = π, **C = πd**, and because d = 2r, **C = 2πr**.
## ✏️ Example 10.5
The radius of a circle is 140 cm. Find a) its diameter b) its circumference (take π = [[22/7]]).
**Solution**
a) d = 2r = 2 × 140 = **280 cm**
b) C = πd = [[22/7]] × 280 = 22 × 40 = **880 cm**
## ✏️ Example 10.6
Find the circumference of circles with these radii, correct to the nearest tenth (take π = 3.142): a) 3.5 cm b) 10 cm c) 4.2 m
**Solution**
a) C = 2 × 3.142 × 3.5 = 21.994 ≈ **22.0 cm**
b) C = 2 × 3.142 × 10 = **62.8 cm** (62.84)
c) C = 2 × 3.142 × 4.2 = 26.3928 ≈ **26.4 m**
## ✏️ Example 10.7
A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 70 cm. How far does the bicycle travel when the wheel turns 50 times? (π = [[22/7]])
**Solution**
One turn: C = [[22/7]] × 70 = 220 cm.
50 turns: 50 × 220 = 11,000 cm = **110 m**

pages.title: Drawing shapes on a square grid
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Draw in a square grid rectangles and triangles with given dimensions.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.1.3
On a square grid each small square has an area of **1 square unit**. Count squares (and half-squares) to find areas.
## ✏️ Example 10.8
The rectangle on the grid measures 3 units by 2 units.
[[fig:m7-f52]]
Figure 10.3: Rectangles on a square grid
a) Draw a rectangle whose area is twice as large. b) Draw a rectangle twice as wide and one and a half times as long.
**Solution**
a) The given area is 3 × 2 = 6 square units, so the new area is 12 square units. Possible rectangles: **4 × 3**, **6 × 2** or **12 × 1**.
b) New width = 2 × 2 = 4 units; new length = 1[[1/2]] × 3 = 4.5 units. Draw a **4.5 by 4** rectangle (area 18 square units).
## ✏️ Example 10.9
a) On a dot grid draw a triangle whose area is 3 square units. b) What is the area of the shaded triangle? How many different triangles with the same area can you draw?
[[fig:m7-f53]]
Figure 10.4: Triangles on a grid
**Solution**
a) A triangle with base 3 units and height 2 units (or base 2 and height 3) has area [[1/2]] × 3 × 2 = **3 square units** — see triangle A.
b) Triangle B has base 4 and height 3; it is half of a 4 × 3 rectangle, so its area is **6 square units**. Keeping the same base and moving the top vertex anywhere along a line parallel to the base keeps the height the same, so **many** different triangles have the same area (every grid point on that line gives one).

pages.title: The area of a triangle
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Use the relationships between a triangle and a rectangle (or parallelogram) to deduce the formula for determining the area of a triangle.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.2.2.1
[[fig:m7-f54|Figure 10.5: Every triangle is half of a rectangle or parallelogram with the same base and height]]
> 🧪 **Activity 10.2 — Cutting rectangles**
1. Draw a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm on paper and cut it out. Draw a diagonal and cut along it. Place the two triangles on top of each other. What do you notice?
2. Draw another 8 cm by 5 cm rectangle. Mark any point on the top side and join it to the two bottom corners. Shade the triangle. Cut out the two unshaded triangles and fit them on the shaded triangle. What fraction of the rectangle is the shaded triangle?
3. Repeat with a parallelogram: draw a diagonal and compare the two triangles.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Area of a triangle** — A triangle is half of a rectangle (or parallelogram) with the same base and perpendicular height. **Area of triangle =** [[1/2]] **× base × perpendicular height =** [[1/2]]**bh.** The **perpendicular height** is measured at right angles to the base, from the opposite vertex (for an obtuse-angled triangle it may fall outside the triangle).

pages.title: Example 10.10
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 10.10
Count the unit squares enclosed by each triangle, state its perpendicular height and find its area.
[[fig:m7-f55]]
Figure 10.6: Triangles on a square grid
**Solution**
a) base 6, perpendicular height 4: enclosing rectangle 6 × 4 = 24, so area = [[1/2]] × 24 = **12 square units**.
b) base 4, perpendicular height 5: area = [[1/2]] × 4 × 5 = **10 square units**.
c) base 3, perpendicular height 4 (measured outside the triangle): area = [[1/2]] × 3 × 4 = **6 square units**.
The perpendicular height tells us the height of the rectangle (or parallelogram) that the triangle is half of — without it we cannot find the area.
**Indicator B7.3.2.2.2** Determine the area of a triangle.
## ✏️ Example 10.11
Calculate the area of each triangle.
[[fig:m7-f56]]
Figure 10.7: Find the area of each triangle
**Solution**
a) [[1/2]] × 8 × 5 = **20 cm²**
b) [[1/2]] × 12 × 7 = **42 cm²**
c) Right-angled: the two shorter sides are base and height: [[1/2]] × 9 × 6 = **27 cm²**
d) Obtuse: base 5 m, height 4 m (outside): [[1/2]] × 5 × 4 = **10 m²**
## ✏️ Example 10.12
The area of a triangle is 36 cm² and its base is 9 cm. Find its height.
**Solution**
[[1/2]] × 9 × h = 36 ⟹ 4.5h = 36 ⟹ **h = 8 cm**
